title: Day 71 · Week 10, Day 1 — Brain: the metal in the wiring — iron for energy, myelin and dopamine, the blood count from the first visit, fifty-seven trials, and the half-million Swedish children
summary: Iron and the unfinished brain. The developing brain can use up to 60% of total metabolic rate, and iron runs three of its jobs — mitochondrial energy, myelination by oligodendrocytes, and dopamine synthesis — with the hippocampus especially exposed (Barks & Georgieff 2018). Most fetal iron moves in the third trimester, but reserves are set now; when iron is short the fetus favours red cells over brain, so anemia is a late sign. Prevalence: 18% of US pregnant women iron deficient, 29.7% in the third trimester (NHANES); >80% by the third trimester in an Irish cohort of 641. ACOG PB 233: CBC in the first trimester and at 24–28 weeks, anemia thresholds Hb <11/10.5/11 g/dL, ferritin <30 µg/L consistent with deficiency, low-dose iron for nearly all. Cochrane 2024 (57 trials, 48,971 women): iron-deficiency anemia at term 5.0% vs 18.4%, low birth weight 5.2% vs 6.1%, no child-brain outcome. Wiegersma 2019 (532,232 Swedish children): anemia diagnosed ≤30 weeks linked to intellectual disability (OR 2.20), autism (1.44) and ADHD (1.37); later anemia was not. The USPSTF 2024 'insufficient' statement and why it doesn't contradict ACOG; RDA 27 mg, UL 45 mg, nausea from iron, alternate-day dosing as emerging, food pairing with vitamin C, and why liver is off the menu.
action: Open the patient portal and find the first-visit blood count. Write the haemoglobin and, if present, the ferritin on the lab page of the Day 61 pregnancy file. If haemoglobin is under 11 g/dL or no ferritin was measured, add to the Questions page: 'Was ferritin checked, and should she be on more than the prenatal's iron?' Check the iron line on the prenatal label, and note if the vitamin is worsening her nausea.
